en: The subduction of the Philippine Sea Plate beneath the Eurasian Plate melts rock, creating magma that feeds volcanoes like Mayon.
The northeast monsoon brings cold, dry air from Siberia to the Philippines, causing the cool amihan season from December to February.
Slightly acidic rainwater dissolves the limestone bedrock of Puerto Princesa, slowly carving out its massive underground cave system over millions of years.
The Cagayan River slows down as it reaches the Babuyan Channel, dropping carried sediments to build a wide, fertile river delta.
Dense mangrove roots along Pampanga Bay trap flowing sediments, which builds up the shoreline and reduces coastal erosion during strong typhoons.
Magma beneath the Albay volcanoes heats groundwater, creating pressure that forces hot steam to the surface to generate geothermal electricity.
The stepped stone walls of the Banaue Rice Terraces slow down rainwater runoff, preventing soil erosion on the steep Cordillera mountainsides.
When ocean temperatures around Tubbataha Reef rise too high, corals expel their colorful algae, causing the reefs to turn completely white.
Taal Volcano erupted and collapsed its own summit, forming a deep caldera that eventually filled with rainwater to create Taal Lake.
Intense tropical sunlight heats the warm waters of the Philippine Sea, causing rapid evaporation that fuels the strong updrafts of approaching typhoons.
Tectonic plates along the Valley Fault System stick together due to friction until built-up stress suddenly snaps, releasing seismic waves that shake the ground.
As a volcanic island in the Sulu Archipelago slowly sinks, growing coral reefs build upward to stay near the sunlight, forming a ring-shaped atoll.
